original_question: What geometric assumptions imply that a metric (possibly, of a fixed signature) on a closed manifold is geodesically complete?
target_in_paper: Section 9.3, Question 9.3.1 ("Completeness of closed manifolds of arbitrary signature," communicated by H. Baum).
correct_elements: The draft already captures the exact target of the paper almost verbatim: it asks for sufficient geometric assumptions guaranteeing geodesic completeness of a metric on a closed manifold, and it preserves the paper's explicit allowance that one may restrict to a fixed signature.
missing_details: The paper's standing convention is that M is a connected C-infinity manifold.

The metric should be understood here in the semi-Riemannian/arbitrary-signature setting; the phrase "possibly, of a fixed signature" means the question may be posed within a prescribed signature class.
The nearby text explicitly defines geodesic completeness: every geodesic gamma:(a,b)->M extends to a geodesic defined on all of R.
To make the question fully stand-alone, "closed manifold" should be spelled out as compact without boundary.

The surrounding context notes that the closed Riemannian case is already classical and automatic, whereas for every indefinite signature there are incomplete metrics on closed manifolds; this is why extra hypotheses are being sought.

The paper is specifically asking for geometric assumptions that are easy to check or that occur for many interesting metrics, not for an arbitrary reformulation or a classification of all complete metrics.
refined_question: Let M be a closed smooth manifold (compact without boundary), and let g be a smooth semi-Riemannian metric on M, possibly restricted to a prescribed signature. Which geometric hypotheses on g, ideally easy to verify or satisfied by broad natural classes of examples, guarantee geodesic completeness in the sense that every geodesic gamma:(a,b)->M extends to a geodesic defined on all of R?
justification: This is the paper's exact Question 9.3.1, with only the nearby hidden assumptions made explicit. The sentence immediately before the question supplies the definition of geodesic completeness, and the preceding context in Section 9 explains that the discussion is about Lorentzian and more generally arbitrary-signature semi-Riemannian metrics. Section 1 supplies the standing smoothness and connectedness conventions for M. I did not replace the draft by the narrower Lorentzian conformal question in 9.3.2, because the paper presents that separately as a specific subquestion rather than as the main target.
